messages.content: I want to predict yeast growth effects for mutation combinations that have not been seen before, across different genetic backgrounds. The goal is also to distinguish epistasis that transfers across backgrounds from interactions that are specific to a background.

That sets up two related questions: how well the growth effect of an unseen combination can be predicted, and whether its nonadditive behavior carries across genetic backgrounds or changes with the background. An interaction can matter to the prediction even if it does not transfer in the same way everywhere.
What should count as the quantitative target for predicting the combinations?

The target is to reduce combination-level root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 10% versus background-aware additive models on unseen genetic backgrounds. The comparison is to an additive baseline that is already background-aware, not to a baseline that ignores genetic background altogether.
Does the 10% refer to a relative reduction in RMSE?

Yes. A 10% reduction means the combination-level RMSE is no more than 90% of the background-aware additive model’s RMSE under the stated comparison. It does not mean subtracting 10 percentage points from an accuracy score: RMSE is an error measure, and lower is better.
And the unseen-background condition is part of that comparison, not just general context?

Right. The stated RMSE target applies on unseen genetic backgrounds. Predicting unseen mutation combinations is the overall task, while the explicit quantitative RMSE comparison is specified for unseen genetic backgrounds.
How should I understand the distinction between transferable epistasis and a background-specific interaction?

Conceptually, transferable epistasis is nonadditive behavior that can inform predictions across backgrounds. A background-specific interaction depends on which genetic background is present. Distinguishing them means not treating every observed interaction as either universally applicable or wholly unrelated to interactions elsewhere. The goal does not specify a particular rule or mechanism for making that distinction.
So transferable does not necessarily mean the effect must have exactly the same size in every background?

Correct. The goal is to distinguish what transfers from what is background-specific; it does not impose exact equality of interaction magnitudes across backgrounds. Nor does it state in advance which interactions will fall into either category.
There is also a target about changes in the sign of epistasis. Can you state that precisely?

The target is to exceed 75% accuracy in identifying epistasis sign changes across backgrounds for independently measurable nonadditive effects. “Exceed” means greater than 75%, not merely equal to it. The condition about independent measurability limits the stated target to nonadditive effects whose signs can be assessed independently.
Is an epistasis sign change the same thing as a growth effect changing from positive to negative?

Not necessarily. Here, the sign belongs to the nonadditive effect: whether the combination departs in one direction or the other from an additive expectation. A sign change across backgrounds concerns that departure, not automatically the sign of the overall growth effect.
Why keep sign-change accuracy separate from combination-level RMSE?

They assess different aspects of the goal. Combination-level RMSE measures the size of prediction errors for growth effects. Sign-change accuracy asks whether the direction of a measurable nonadditive effect is correctly identified as changing across backgrounds. A prediction could be close in magnitude yet miss an important change in interaction sign, so the two targets should not be collapsed into one.
Does the sign-change target cover every possible interaction?

No. Its stated scope is epistasis sign changes across backgrounds for independently measurable nonadditive effects. It would overstate the requirement to claim that the greater-than-75% accuracy target covers effects whose nonadditivity cannot be independently measured.
Would meeting only the RMSE target fully express the goal?

No. The goal includes distinguishing transferable epistasis from background-specific interactions, and it gives a separate threshold for identifying sign changes. The 10% RMSE reduction addresses predictive error on unseen genetic backgrounds; the greater-than-75% sign-change accuracy addresses a particular aspect of how nonadditive effects vary across backgrounds.
I want to make sure the baseline is described without weakening it. Is “an additive model” specific enough?

For the numerical requirement, it is important to say “background-aware additive models.” Calling the baseline simply “an additive model” leaves out a stated part of the comparison and could make the 10% reduction sound easier to achieve than specified.
Can you put the whole goal into one careful statement?

Predict yeast growth effects of unseen mutation combinations across genetic backgrounds while distinguishing transferable epistasis from background-specific interactions. On unseen genetic backgrounds, reduce combination-level RMSE by 10% relative to background-aware additive models, and exceed 75% accuracy in identifying epistasis sign changes across backgrounds for independently measurable nonadditive effects.
What kind of model would let us make that distinction while predicting growth?

A proposal is to fit a pathway-regularized hierarchical growth model. It would separate transferable mutation-pair effects from genotype-conditioned residuals, with those residuals able to represent epistasis sign reversals.
What does “hierarchical” mean in this proposal?

It refers to representing the effects at more than one level: a mutation-pair effect that can transfer across genetic backgrounds, alongside a residual conditioned on genotype. The distinction lets the model express both a shared pattern and departures from that pattern in particular genetic contexts.
If there is a transferable pair effect, is the proposal assuming that the pair behaves identically in every background?

No. The transferable effect captures what may be shared, while the genotype-conditioned residual allows the pair’s nonadditive behavior to differ by context. Calling an effect transferable does not require the complete effect in every background to be identical.
Why specify mutation-pair effects rather than just saying the model has transferable effects?

It identifies the level at which the proposed shared component represents interactions: mutation pairs. That makes the separation more precise. The model is meant to distinguish a pair-level contribution that transfers from the part of the interaction that depends on genotype.
How does the genotype-conditioned residual relate to a sign reversal?

The residual can change the nonadditive effect associated with a mutation pair in a particular genotype. If it shifts that effect far enough in the opposite direction, the resulting epistasis can have the opposite sign from its value in another background. The proposal permits such reversals; it does not presume that every pair reverses sign.
So “residual” does not mean something the model simply ignores?

Right. Here the residual is a modeled, genotype-conditioned component. It represents context-dependent behavior left after accounting for the transferable mutation-pair effect, rather than being a label for interactions the model cannot address.
Would a model with only transferable pair effects be enough for the stated distinction?

Not for the distinction as proposed. Shared pair effects alone would not explicitly represent genotype-conditioned departures, including possible epistasis sign reversals. The separate residual component is what allows the model to express those background-specific interactions.
What role does pathway regularization play?

It introduces pathway-informed regularization into the growth model. In broad terms, that means using pathway structure to guide how effects are fit, rather than treating the interaction terms as entirely unconstrained. The proposal does not specify the particular pathway information, the mathematical form of the regularization, or its strength.
Does pathway regularization mean that an interaction outside a pathway would be ruled out?

That is not stated. “Regularized” indicates that pathway information influences the fit, but this proposal does not say that effects must be confined to pathways or that any particular interaction is forbidden. Those would be additional modeling choices.
I also don't want to imply that the pathway component already explains the sign changes.

That would go beyond the proposal. Pathway regularization is part of the suggested model, while genotype-conditioned residuals are the component explicitly described as permitting epistasis sign reversals. Whether the model successfully explains or predicts such changes remains to be evaluated.
Is this a fitted result or a modeling plan?
It is a proposal to fit the model, not a report that it has been fitted or that any performance target has been achieved.
Can you restate the proposal without promising what it will accomplish?

Fit a pathway-regularized hierarchical model of yeast growth that represents transferable mutation-pair effects separately from genotype-conditioned residuals. The residuals would allow epistasis to reverse sign across genetic backgrounds, without assuming that such reversals occur for every pair or that the proposed model will predict them successfully.
How can replicated growth measurements distinguish genuine background-dependent epistasis sign reversals from noise in pathway-regularized residuals?

Replicates give a way to estimate how much the measured growth effects vary even when the genetic background and mutation combination are the same. That measurement variability can then be considered when estimating the nonadditive effect in each background. A reversal is more convincing when the estimated epistasis has opposite signs across backgrounds and those signs remain credible after accounting for the variability in the measurements—not merely because fitted residuals happen to cross zero.
Why isn't an opposite sign in the fitted residuals enough?

The residual is only the genotype-conditioned part of the model. Epistasis in a given background also includes the transferable mutation-pair effect, so a residual changing sign does not necessarily mean the overall nonadditive effect changes sign. And even if the fitted overall effects have opposite signs, a small difference driven by noisy measurements would not by itself establish a genuine reversal.
What exactly would the replicates need to tell us?

They need to inform the uncertainty around the growth measurements used to assess nonadditivity in each background. The question is whether an apparent departure from the additive expectation is distinguishable from measurement variation, and whether its direction is distinguishable in both backgrounds. Replicates of a combination alone do not establish epistasis unless the relevant additive expectation can also be estimated.
Could the same mutation pair show an apparent reversal just because its effect is near zero?

Yes. When a nonadditive effect is near zero, modest measurement variation can change its estimated sign. Opposite point estimates in two backgrounds can therefore look like a reversal even though the measurements do not clearly distinguish either effect from zero. Reporting uncertainty alongside the estimated signs is important for separating that situation from a well-supported reversal.
Would requiring the uncertainty range for each effect to stay on its respective side of zero be a reasonable way to think about it?

It is a clear, conservative illustration: if the nonadditive effect in one background is credibly on one side of zero and the effect in another is credibly on the other, the sign reversal has direct measurement support. The question does not prescribe that particular decision rule, however. Whatever rule is used should account for uncertainty in the nonadditive effects, rather than relying only on the signs of fitted estimates.
Where does pathway regularization enter that judgment?

Pathway regularization influences the fitted effects, including how the model balances a transferable mutation-pair effect against genotype-conditioned departures. It does not make a sign reversal genuine merely by producing a stable-looking fitted residual. Replicated growth measurements provide a check on whether the background-dependent nonadditivity represented by the model is distinguishable from measurement noise.
So should we treat regularization and replication as answering different questions?

Yes. Regularization guides the fit of the model; replication helps assess variability in the underlying growth measurements. A pathway-regularized model can represent a sign reversal, but the measurements must support the direction of the nonadditive effect in the relevant backgrounds before calling that reversal genuine.
If repeated measurements vary a lot, does that prove there is no background-dependent interaction?

No. High variability can make an interaction or sign reversal difficult to distinguish from noise; it does not prove that the interaction is absent. The careful conclusion would be that the available measurements do not resolve its sign reliably, rather than that its true effect must be zero or must have the same sign across backgrounds.
And if the repetitions are consistent, does that settle it?

Consistency strengthens the case, but the relevant consistency is in the estimated nonadditive effects relative to their additive expectations, not just in the raw growth measurements. One would still need to check that the overall epistasis, rather than only a model residual, is supported as having opposite signs across backgrounds.
Can you state the distinction in one sentence?

A genuine background-dependent epistasis sign reversal is supported when replicated growth measurements distinguish oppositely signed nonadditive effects across backgrounds from measurement variability; opposite signs in pathway-regularized residual estimates alone are not sufficient.
Could we make the distinction between a sign reversal and noise more concrete using uncertainty in both backgrounds?

One hypothesis is that requiring 95% credible intervals to exclude zero in both backgrounds will yield at least 80% sign-reversal concordance across independent growth-assay batches. It is a proposed criterion and a predicted outcome, not an observed level of concordance.
For a sign reversal, do the two intervals also need to be on opposite sides of zero?

Yes. Excluding zero in both backgrounds indicates support for a nonzero effect in each, but does not by itself indicate a reversal. For the proposed sign-reversal criterion, the nonadditive effects would have opposite signs: the credible interval in one background would lie on one side of zero, and the interval in the other background would lie on the other.
Why require that level of support in both backgrounds rather than just one?

A reversal makes a claim about the direction of nonadditivity in each background. If the effect in either background remains compatible with zero, an apparent difference in signs could be driven by uncertainty around that effect. Requiring 95% credible intervals excluding zero in both backgrounds is a way to focus on reversals whose two signs are individually distinguishable from zero.
What is the predicted outcome of using that requirement?

The hypothesis predicts sign-reversal concordance of ≥80% across independent growth-assay batches among reversals that meet the stated credible-interval requirement. The ≥ symbol matters: 80% would meet the predicted threshold, as would a higher value.
What does concordance across batches mean here?

It concerns whether a sign-reversal call agrees when assessed using independent growth-assay batches. The hypothesis is that the calls passing the two-background uncertainty criterion will agree across those batches at least 80% of the time. It does not say that every individual call must agree in every batch.
Are the 95% and 80% figures two ways of expressing the same probability?

No. The 95% figure describes the credible intervals used to judge whether the nonadditive effect excludes zero in each background. The ≥80% figure is a prediction about concordance of sign-reversal calls across independent growth-assay batches. One does not automatically follow numerically from the other; their proposed relationship is what the hypothesis puts forward.
Does having a 95% credible interval in each background mean there is automatically 95% certainty about the reversal as a whole?

Not automatically. The condition concerns two individual effect intervals, each excluding zero and lying on opposite sides of it. That should not be silently turned into a claim that the joint sign-reversal event has a 95% probability, or that batch-to-batch concordance is guaranteed. The predicted ≥80% concordance is separate and would need to be assessed across independent batches.
How does this address the concern about noise in pathway-regularized residuals?

It makes the evidence for a reversal depend on uncertainty around the nonadditive effects in both backgrounds, rather than on opposite signs appearing in fitted residuals alone. Independent growth-assay batches then provide a check on whether calls made under that criterion agree beyond one batch. The hypothesis does not assert that the criterion eliminates noise or that it has already passed that check.
If an effect's credible interval crosses zero in one background, should that automatically be called no epistasis?

No. Under the hypothesized criterion, that comparison would not qualify as a supported sign-reversal call, because one of the two signs is not distinguished from zero by its 95% credible interval. That is not the same as establishing that epistasis is absent in that background.
And if both intervals exclude zero but lie on the same side?
Then the two effects satisfy the exclusion-from-zero part of the criterion but not the opposite-sign part. They would not constitute a sign reversal between those backgrounds.
Could you restate the hypothesis without making it sound like a completed result?

The hypothesis is that, for epistasis sign reversals supported by 95% credible intervals excluding zero in both backgrounds and indicating opposite signs, sign-reversal concordance will be ≥80% across independent growth-assay batches. Whether that predicted concordance holds remains an empirical question.
How would we test the idea that the credible sign reversals are reproducible rather than noise?

The plan is to measure single mutations and mutation pairs across eight genetic backgrounds in independent growth-assay batches, then test whether sign reversals meeting the 95%-credible criterion achieve ≥80% concordance across batches. That is a planned test, not a reported result.
Why measure singles as well as pairs?

The single-mutation measurements help establish the additive expectation against which a pair’s growth effect is assessed. Without that comparison, a pair’s measured growth alone would not establish the sign of its nonadditive effect. Measuring both across the backgrounds therefore speaks directly to whether an apparent epistasis sign reversal is supported.
And why are there eight backgrounds in the plan?

Eight is the stated number of genetic backgrounds across which singles and pairs are to be measured. It makes the test explicitly about variation across backgrounds, rather than only a contrast within one background. The plan does not specify why eight was chosen or claim that eight is a generally sufficient number.
What work do the independent batches do that the eight backgrounds do not?

The backgrounds provide the genetic contexts in which an effect might change sign. The independent batches provide a way to ask whether a sign-reversal call agrees across separate sets of growth-assay measurements. Those are different comparisons: variation across backgrounds is the phenomenon of interest, while agreement across batches is the reproducibility check.
When you say a “95%-credible reversal,” what exactly would be checked?

It refers to the proposed uncertainty criterion: the 95% credible interval for the nonadditive effect excludes zero in each of the two backgrounds being compared, with the intervals indicating opposite signs. The planned test then asks whether reversals meeting that criterion show ≥80% concordance across independent batches.
Does an interval excluding zero in both backgrounds, by itself, qualify?

No. Both effects could be credibly nonzero yet have the same sign. A sign reversal also requires opposite directions of nonadditivity across the backgrounds. The intervals excluding zero support the individual signs; they do not replace the opposite-sign requirement.
Would every pair measured across the eight backgrounds necessarily become a credible reversal?

No. The plan is to measure singles and pairs across eight backgrounds and assess the resulting effects. It does not presume that every mutation pair is nonadditive, that every nonadditive effect reverses sign, or that every apparent reversal satisfies the 95%-credible criterion.
Suppose the measurements suggest opposite signs, but one credible interval includes zero. How does that fit into this test?

That comparison would not meet the stated 95%-credible reversal criterion. It might remain an apparent reversal worth describing as uncertain, but counting it as one of the criterion-qualified reversals would blur the distinction the test is meant to examine.
Does ≥80% concordance mean the batches must give identical growth values?

No. The threshold concerns concordance of sign-reversal calls across independent growth-assay batches, not identical numerical growth measurements. Differences in measured values can occur while the assessed directions of the nonadditive effects still agree.
Should we say in advance that this will distinguish genuine reversals from noise?

We can say the measurements and independent batches are intended to test that distinction. We should not say they have already established it. The plan specifically tests whether reversals supported by the 95% credible-interval criterion reach ≥80% batch-to-batch concordance.
Does this plan also specify how the pathway-regularized growth model will be fitted?

No. It specifies measurements of singles and pairs across eight backgrounds in independent batches and a concordance test for 95%-credible reversals. It does not provide additional fitting details for the pathway-regularized model. The measurement plan can bear on whether inferred background-dependent sign changes are reproducible without itself specifying the model-fitting procedure.
Give me a concise version of the plan that keeps the test and its threshold explicit.

Measure single mutations and mutation pairs across eight genetic backgrounds in independent growth-assay batches, then test whether epistasis sign reversals meeting the 95%-credible criterion achieve ≥80% concordance across those batches.
What is the concrete assay activity for checking these sign reversals?

Assay 120 mutation pairs and their constituent single mutations across eight genetic backgrounds in two batches, then calculate concordance for 95%-credible epistasis sign reversals. The activity specifies what to measure and what to calculate; it does not give a concordance value.
Are the constituent singles part of the 120 mutation pairs, or are they additional measurements?

The 120 refers to mutation pairs. Their constituent singles are also to be assayed so the pairs’ growth effects can be compared with an additive expectation. The activity does not specify a separate count of distinct single mutations; different pairs could have singles in common.
Why do the single-mutation measurements matter for this calculation?

A sign reversal concerns the nonadditive effect of a mutation pair, not just whether the pair’s measured growth increases or decreases. The singles help establish the additive expectation in a genetic background, so the pair can be assessed for a departure from that expectation. The direction of that departure is the epistasis sign at issue.
What separate purposes do the eight backgrounds and the two batches serve?

The eight backgrounds provide the genetic contexts across which epistasis might change sign. The two batches provide separate sets of growth-assay measurements for assessing whether a 95%-credible reversal call is concordant across batches. A difference across backgrounds is the potential biological pattern; agreement across batches is the reproducibility question.
Does measuring 120 pairs mean there will be 120 sign reversals to compare?

No. The 120 pairs are the assay scope, not a count of reversals. A pair might show no independently distinguishable nonadditive effect, might retain the same sign across backgrounds, or might have an apparent change whose uncertainty prevents it from meeting the 95%-credible criterion. The activity does not state how many qualifying reversals there will be.
Remind me what makes a reversal 95%-credible here.

For the backgrounds being compared, the proposed criterion requires the 95% credible interval for the nonadditive effect to exclude zero in each background, with the effects on opposite sides of zero. Excluding zero in both backgrounds supports the individual signs; their being opposite is what makes it a reversal.
Would a change in the sign of a pathway-regularized residual be counted on its own?

No. The sign-reversal question concerns the nonadditive effect in each background, not merely the genotype-conditioned residual component of a fitted model. The assay of pairs and constituent singles bears on those background-specific nonadditive effects; a residual crossing zero alone would not establish that the effects themselves reverse sign.
What if both effects look nonzero but have the same sign?
Then they do not constitute a sign reversal between those backgrounds, even if their 95% credible intervals both exclude zero. The criterion requires opposite signs as well as support for each sign.
And if the point estimates have opposite signs, but one interval includes zero?

That would be an apparent reversal, but it would not qualify as a 95%-credible reversal under the stated criterion. The interval including zero leaves the sign of one nonadditive effect unresolved for this purpose; it does not prove that the effect is absent.
When we calculate concordance, are we asking whether the measured growth numbers are identical in the two batches?

No. Concordance here concerns agreement of sign-reversal assessments across the two batches, not equality of the numerical growth measurements. Measurements can differ without necessarily changing the assessed signs of the nonadditive effects.
Do we know from this activity exactly how every eligible background comparison will enter the concordance calculation?

No. The activity says to calculate 95%-credible reversal concordance after assaying the pairs and singles across eight backgrounds in two batches. It does not specify the detailed counting rule for background comparisons or how to handle every possible pattern of uncertainty between batches. Those details should not be assumed from the assay counts alone.
What is the point of calculating that concordance?

It supplies the batch-to-batch quantity for evaluating the proposed ≥80% concordance prediction for 95%-credible reversals. The specified activity is to calculate it; neither the number of qualifying reversals nor the resulting concordance is stated here.
What did the comparison across batches show for the credible sign reversals?
Among 64 reversals identified in batch one with 95% credible intervals excluding zero, 42 replicated in batch two. That is 66% when rounded to a whole percent.
Is 64 the number of mutation pairs that were assayed?

No. The 64 is the number of qualifying batch-one reversals in this result. It should not be read as the total number of assayed mutation pairs or as a count of all possible comparisons across backgrounds.
So which batch determines what goes into that group of 64?

Batch one does. The result starts with 64 reversals that had 95% credible intervals excluding zero in batch one, then asks how many of those replicated in batch two. It does not give the number of reversals that might be identified by starting with batch two instead.
Does the 95% credible-interval condition refer to the signs in both backgrounds of a reversal?

Yes, in the stated sign-reversal criterion, each of the two backgrounds being compared has a nonadditive effect whose 95% credible interval excludes zero, and the effects have opposite signs. This result identifies 64 batch-one reversals meeting that condition. It does not provide the individual effect estimates or intervals.
What does the 42 count represent?

It is the number of those 64 batch-one reversals that replicated in batch two. The remaining 22 did not replicate under the reported comparison. The result does not specify what happened in each of those 22 cases.
Can I say the other 22 definitely had the opposite pattern in batch two?

No. “Did not replicate” does not tell us whether a sign changed, an effect became too uncertain to classify, or something else prevented a matching reversal call. The evidence gives the replication count, not a breakdown of the nonreplicating cases.
And does replication mean batch two measured exactly the same growth effects?

No. The reported outcome is that the reversal replicated in batch two, not that the numerical growth measurements or estimated effect sizes were identical between batches. No batch-two effect sizes are given here.
How is the reported percentage calculated?
It uses the 64 qualifying batch-one reversals as the denominator: 42 divided by 64 is 0.65625, reported as 66% after rounding. It is not a percentage of every assayed pair.
Do these data tell us which reversals are transferable and which are background-specific?

Not individually. This result concerns whether batch-one sign reversals replicated in batch two. It does not identify particular mutation pairs, quantify transferable pair effects, or give a pair-by-pair account of genotype-conditioned residuals.
What is the most careful way to describe what we learned from the second batch?

The second batch replicated 42 of the 64 batch-one reversals whose 95% credible intervals excluded zero, for a reported concordance of 66%. That describes the observed batch-to-batch result without assuming why the other reversals did not replicate.
Can we state a more selective hypothesis about which sign reversals will replicate across batches?

The revised hypothesis is that discovery-batch reversals with 99% credible intervals and nonadditive effect magnitudes of at least 0.05 log-growth units in both backgrounds will replicate at a rate of ≥80% across batches. That is a prediction to test, not a measured replication rate.
What does “discovery-batch reversals” mean in that statement?

It means the reversals are identified using a discovery batch, and the hypothesis concerns whether those selected reversals replicate across batches. Selection and replication play different roles: a call qualifies in the discovery batch; agreement in another batch is the outcome being predicted.
Does the 0.05 threshold apply to the difference between the two backgrounds?

No. The wording says the effect must be at least 0.05 log-growth units in both backgrounds. For an epistasis sign reversal, the nonadditive effects have opposite signs, and the magnitude requirement applies to each effect separately—not merely to the distance between them.
So one background cannot have a substantial effect while the other is nearly zero?

Not if the reversal is to qualify under this hypothesis. Each background must meet the ≥0.05 log-growth-unit effect-magnitude requirement. A strong effect in one background would not make up for an effect below that threshold in the other.
How should I read the 99% credible-interval part?

It is an uncertainty requirement for the discovery-batch reversal. In this context, the intervals must support opposite signs for the nonadditive effects in the two backgrounds, with each interval excluding zero; otherwise they would not establish a credible sign reversal. The 99% level concerns those intervals, not the predicted percentage that will replicate across batches.
Is ≥0.05 log-growth units a threshold on overall yeast growth?

No. It refers to the effects involved in the epistasis sign reversal—the nonadditive effects in the two backgrounds—not simply the overall growth measurement for a mutation pair. Keeping that distinction matters because the sign being checked is the sign of epistasis.
If the estimated effects are +0.05 and −0.05 log-growth units, would their magnitudes meet the effect-size condition?

Yes. Each magnitude would equal 0.05 log-growth units, so each would meet a ≥0.05 condition. To qualify as a discovery-batch reversal under the full hypothesis, their 99% credible intervals would also need to support those opposite signs.
What if both magnitudes clear 0.05, but one 99% credible interval includes zero?

Then the estimates meet the magnitude condition, but the interval does not establish the sign of one effect under the stated credibility condition. It should not be counted as a qualifying 99%-credible discovery-batch reversal on the strength of the point estimates alone.
And what if both intervals exclude zero but the effects have the same sign?
That would not be a sign reversal. Credible nonzero effects and sufficiently large magnitudes are not substitutes for the requirement that epistasis have opposite signs across the two backgrounds.
Why include both an interval condition and a minimum effect magnitude?

They screen for different things. A 99% credible interval supporting a sign addresses uncertainty about the direction of an effect. The ≥0.05 log-growth-unit condition requires the nonadditive effect in each background to reach a stated magnitude. The hypothesis proposes that reversals satisfying both conditions in the discovery batch will show ≥80% replication across batches; it does not establish that they will.
Does “≥80%” mean every qualifying discovery-batch reversal must replicate?

No. It predicts a replication rate of at least 80% across batches for the qualifying discovery-batch reversals. It allows for some individual calls not to replicate. Exactly how many calls qualify, and the observed replication rate, are not specified by the hypothesis.
Does the hypothesis say the 99% interval and 0.05 threshold must also be met independently in every other batch?

It explicitly describes the reversals selected in the discovery batch and predicts that they will replicate across batches. It does not spell out a separate numerical qualification rule for every other batch, so that detail should not be added to the hypothesis as though it were stated.
Can this hypothesis alone tell us that a pathway-regularized residual is a genuine background-specific interaction?

No. It proposes a reproducibility test for sign reversals in nonadditive effects measured across backgrounds. A fitted residual changing sign on its own is not the same as an effect meeting the discovery-batch credibility and magnitude conditions, and the predicted ≥80% cross-batch replication remains to be tested.
Please give me a compact statement that preserves every threshold.

Hypothesis: discovery-batch epistasis sign reversals supported by 99% credible intervals and by nonadditive effects of magnitude ≥0.05 log-growth units in both backgrounds will replicate at a rate of ≥80% across batches.
What is the next analysis for the 64 batch-one reversals?

Reanalyze those 64 batch-one reversals using 99% credible intervals and a minimum nonadditive effect magnitude of 0.05 log-growth units in both backgrounds. Then assess batch-two concordance for the reversals that meet those conditions. This describes an analysis to perform, not its outcome.
Are we looking for a new set of reversals from every pair that was assayed?

No. The specified starting set is the 64 batch-one reversals. The reanalysis asks which of those meet the 99% credible-interval and effect-magnitude conditions, then examines their concordance with batch two. It does not specify a new search across all assayed pairs.
How should the 99% credible intervals be used when deciding whether a reversal qualifies?

For a credible sign reversal, the nonadditive effects in the two backgrounds need supported opposite signs. That means the 99% credible interval for each effect excludes zero, with the intervals lying on opposite sides of zero. Opposite-signed point estimates alone would not meet that interval condition.
Does the 0.05 requirement apply separately to each background?
Yes. The nonadditive effect must have magnitude ≥0.05 log-growth units in both backgrounds. An effect meeting the threshold in one background cannot compensate for an effect below it in the other.
Is 0.05 included, or does the magnitude have to be greater than 0.05?
It is included: ≥0.05 log-growth units means at least 0.05. The credible-interval condition must also be met; reaching the magnitude threshold by itself does not qualify a reversal.
Would taking the difference between the two background effects be enough to check the magnitude condition?
No. A large difference could occur even if one background’s nonadditive effect has magnitude below 0.05 log-growth units. The stated condition applies to each background’s effect separately.
What if both effects have sufficient magnitude but their 99% intervals are on the same side of zero?
They would not form a qualifying sign reversal. The reanalysis requires opposite signs as well as sufficient magnitude and credible support for each sign.
And if one 99% interval crosses zero despite its point estimate meeting 0.05?
It would not satisfy the 99%-credible reversal condition. A point estimate can meet the magnitude threshold while its interval still leaves the sign unresolved under that criterion.
What is the denominator when assessing batch-two concordance?

It should be the batch-one reversals from the specified set of 64 that qualify under the reanalysis conditions—not automatically all 64. Concordance then concerns how many of those qualifying calls replicate in batch two. The activity does not state how many will qualify or how many will replicate.
Are we applying the 99% and 0.05 cutoffs to batch two as well?

The activity explicitly says to reanalyze the 64 batch-one reversals using those conditions and to assess batch-two concordance. It does not specify an additional rule that batch two must independently pass the same cutoffs, so that detail should not be assumed.
Can we calculate the new concordance from the information we have already discussed?
No. We would need to know which of the 64 batch-one reversals meet both reanalysis conditions and which of those are concordant in batch two. Neither count is given in the activity.
How does this analysis relate to the proposed replication threshold?

The resulting batch-two concordance would be the quantity used to assess the prediction of ≥80% replication for reversals meeting the 99% credible-interval and ≥0.05 log-growth-unit conditions in both backgrounds. The reanalysis itself does not say whether that threshold is reached.
Can you state the activity in one sentence without implying a result?

Reanalyze the 64 batch-one epistasis sign reversals, retaining those supported by 99% credible intervals and nonadditive effects of magnitude ≥0.05 log-growth units in both backgrounds, then assess their concordance in batch two.
What did the reanalysis show for batch-one reversals meeting both stricter criteria?

Thirty batch-one reversals met both criteria: 99% credible intervals supporting opposite nonadditive-effect signs and effect magnitudes of at least 0.05 log-growth units in both backgrounds. Of those 30, 26 replicated in batch two, giving 87% concordance when rounded to a whole percent.
Is 87% calculated from the 30 qualifying reversals?
Yes. The calculation is 26 divided by 30, or approximately 86.7%, reported as 87%. The denominator is the reversals that met both stricter criteria in batch one.
